evidence.title: Current safeguards, risk mitigation, and transparency measures of large language models against the generation of health disinformation: repeated cross sectional analysis
evidence.outcome: Developer responsiveness to reported safeguard vulnerabilities
evidence.effect: Each LLM had reporting mechanisms, but developers did not respond when vulnerabilities were reported.
evidence.quote: Although each LLM evaluated had mechanisms to report observed outputs of concern, the developers did not respond when observations of vulnerabilities were reported.

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether bidirectional reporting channels between health systems and AI vendors improve how harms, performance findings, vulnerabilities, or recalls are communicated or acted on. One descriptive study found that large language model developers had reporting mechanisms but did not respond when vulnerabilities were reported, which suggests that a channel's existence alone may not ensure a response.

perspectives.view: Four sources endorse the practice, and none of them reports outcome data. The only study is a level 4 descriptive assessment in a simulated setting in Australia, and it documents the hazard rather than testing the practice. Under GRADE conventions this leaves no direct evidence on whether bidirectional channels change reporting, correction, or patient outcomes.

In the hazard study, each model had a reporting mechanism, yet developers did not respond to reported safeguard vulnerabilities. A channel that accepts reports without returning a response or a fix may leave the failure uncorrected. The study suggests that response times and confirmation of fixes may matter as much as the intake route, though no study has measured this.

The endorsements range from sharing configuration changes and returning corrected AI results to vendors, to a manufacturer-maintained reporting route linked from FDA public summaries and labeling. One framework advises that contracts keep reporter identity from vendors during root-cause analysis. No study examines whether contract terms or labeling-linked routes produce vendor action.

A patient harmed by an AI tool depends on the report reaching someone who can fix it. The hazard study found that developers did not answer reported vulnerabilities even though reporting routes existed. Patients and staff who report problems may lose trust if their reports receive no reply, and no study has tested how to prevent this.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems with and without structured vendor reporting agreements. These studies should measure vendor response rates, time to acknowledgment and correction, how often recalls or updates reach frontline users, and whether reporters' confidentiality is maintained.
commentary.underserved_note: The single hazard study was conducted in a simulated setting in Australia and did not include Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. No evidence shows whether harms affecting these groups are reported or corrected through vendor channels at the same rate as harms affecting other patients.
